title: When does change become a revolution? Why Britain?

review.note: Built from Mr Garry's own lessons for this unit (2026–27 scheme of work). Check wording against the lesson PowerPoints before relying on it.

learn.intro: Britain in 1750 was mostly rural; by 1900 it was the world's first industrialised, majority-urban nation. But calling this a "revolution" is a historian's judgement, not a fact. This topic gives you the tools to judge it (Scale, Speed, Depth, Duration) and asks why industrialisation began in Britain.

sections.title: 1. Change, continuity and revolution

blocks.p: In 1750 roughly three-quarters of people worked on the land, most goods were made by hand in homes or small workshops, and travel was slow and local. By 1900 most people worked in industry and lived in towns, and railways crossed the country in hours. England's population grew from around 6 million in 1750 to over 30 million by 1900.
The phrase "Industrial Revolution" was popularised by historians looking back, notably Arnold Toynbee in the 1880s. It is a later label and an argument that needs evidence.

Judge with the four criteria: Scale (how many people), Speed (how quickly), Depth (how fundamentally lives changed), Duration (how lasting). You will track every development in the unit against these criteria in your Revolution Tracker.
Two traps: change is not the same as progress (it can make things worse for some people), and "revolutionary" does not mean "positive".

evidence: England: about 6 million people in 1750; over 30 million by 1900.

sections.title: 2. Why Britain?

blocks.p: Historians reject a single cause in favour of interconnected causes, a "perfect storm":

ul: Agriculture: more food meant fewer farm workers were needed, freeing labour for industry.
Population: England's population roughly doubled during the 18th century, supplying workers and consumers.
Coal: large, accessible reserves powered steam engines and furnaces.
Capital: money from farming, banking, merchant trade and Atlantic and colonial trade, including trade linked to the enslavement of Africans (explored in the next topic).
Transport: turnpike roads and canals from the 1760s (the Bridgewater Canal opened in 1761) moved goods cheaply.
Institutions: stable government, secure property rights and patent law gave inventors and investors confidence.

blocks.p: Older stories credited a few "great inventors". Historians now stress how these causes reinforced each other.

evidence: Causes were interconnected, not a list.

exam.criteria_note: Practice questions written for this unit. AI feedback is formative only (no marks) until department KS3 criteria are added.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "Coal was the main reason industrialisation began in Britain." How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Weigh coal against other causes and show how they interconnected.
steps: Explain at least two other causes and how they linked.
questions.plan: 3 minutes planning, 11 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.

model.t: Coal was highly important, but only to some extent the main reason, because it worked with other causes.
Coal powered steam engines such as Watt's (patented 1769), but canals like the Bridgewater Canal (1761) were needed to move it cheaply.
This meant coal only became decisive once transport and capital allowed it to be used on a large scale.
Therefore industrialisation resulted from interconnected causes, with coal as a necessary but not sufficient one.

full: P: Coal was the main reason to a large / some extent because…
E: This meant that… However, it depended on…
some: P – Topic sentence with a qualifier (blue): One key reason … / To a large extent … / On the other hand …
E – Precisely selected evidence (purple), in order with time connectives (green): At the start … / Later … / Eventually … / Finally …
E – Explain with arguing connectives (red): However … / This was more important because … / In contrast …
J – Judgement: This shows that … / Overall, the most important reason was … / Therefore, I agree to a large/limited extent …
